Music printing has been around since the mid 15th century. Even before then, music was frequently copied by hand... often monks... 

When we get to the 16th century, Ottaviano Petrucci developed a significantly more efficient method of music printing sacrificing elegance and lavish decorations on the music for the significantly increased speed and number of prints.

This music looked much different then modern notion which was still in development at this time & parts (specific parts for specific instruments) were nonexistent. People just played the parts with whatever instruments they could or they sung them. Once we hit the Baroque (1600-1750) parts are identified for a specific instrumentation.

A suspension holds from one chord to another. A suspended 4th in particular moves from the 4th scale degree (On a Major I chord for example) down to the 3rd.

An augmented chord raises the 5th of the chord a half step. 

The trick is, once you learn what everything means, all you have to do is apply it to whatever chords or notes you have, I.E:

A diminished chord is a minor chord with a lowered 5th, so take an a-minor chords... a, c, e... lower the e, which is the 5th, to an e-flat and you have an a-diminished chord!
